item.title: java concurrency - thread pool and BlockingQueue
item.description:
A Java thread pool separates task submission from task execution. Submitting threads hand Runnable objects to an ExecutorService; a set of worker threads removes those tasks and runs them. In ThreadPoolExecutor and ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor the hand-off point between the two sides is a java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue<Runnable>. The queue therefore decides how tasks are buffered, ordered and throttled, and the pool decides how many threads consume them.

This article first enumerates the thread pool and blocking queue types of the JDK. Part 1 then examines the OpenJDK BlockingQueue implementations: the dual-condition bounded buffer, the two-lock design of LinkedBlockingQueue, the heap-backed PriorityBlockingQueue, the zero-capacity rendezvous of SynchronousQueue, and the timed waiting protocol of DelayQueue. Part 2 examines the thread pools built on them: the control state, admission, worker loop, rejection and shutdown of ThreadPoolExecutor, the Executors factories, and the scheduling of ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor.

item.title: Java ConcurrentHashMap implementation
item.description:
java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap is a highly concurrent, thread-safe hash table in the Java Collections Framework. It allows full concurrency of retrievals and high expected concurrency for updates. Unlike HashMap, it prohibits null keys and values to avoid the ambiguity of get(key) == null.

The design avoids table-wide locks: reads are lock-free via volatile fields; writes use CAS on empty bins and synchronized on the bin head; resizing is cooperative — threads that encounter a ForwardingNode help migrate bins rather than blocking.

item.title: Java HashMap implementation
item.description:
java.util.HashMap is a hash table-based implementation of the Map interface in the Java Collections Framework, permitting null keys and null values. It is not thread-safe — concurrent updates require external synchronization or ConcurrentHashMap.

At a high level, every operation follows the same path: spread the key’s hash, mask it to a bin index, then search or mutate the bin’s chain (or tree). When the table grows too full, resize() doubles capacity and re-distributes entries.

item.title: Data structure — trees
item.description: Trees are hierarchical structures in which each node has a parent (except the root) and zero or more children. This article records the principal binary-tree variants, their defining properties, array-based layouts, and typical applications — including the complete binary tree backing a binary heap and the red-black tree used in TreeMap, TreeSet, and HashMap tree bins.
